blocks.text: 1. Frozen Layers

blocks.alt: A pretrained model has frozen layers with no updates and trainable layers that get updated

blocks.text: Fine-Tuning, the previous topic, introduced the choice between updating every weight or only some. Frozen Layers give a closer look at which weights actually get updated during Fine-Tuning, explored throughout this topic.
It works by deliberately keeping some pretrained layers genuinely fixed, unchanged throughout Fine-Tuning, a genuinely practical technique covered throughout the rest of this topic.
2. Recapping The Partial Fine-Tuning Choice

This connects back to full versus partial Fine-Tuning, already covered in Fine-Tuning. Fine-Tuning can genuinely update every single weight, or genuinely only some of them, already covered there in general terms.
This topic genuinely explores exactly how that partial approach actually works, giving that earlier general observation its own complete, dedicated treatment.
3. What Freezing Genuinely Means

blocks.alt: Weights receive no gradient updates when frozen

blocks.text: The genuinely core idea connects back to Gradient Descent's own update rule, already covered in its own topic. A frozen layer's own weights genuinely never get updated, even though gradients still genuinely flow through it.
This genuinely precise definition, already covered in this section, distinguishes freezing from genuinely removing a layer entirely: a frozen layer still genuinely participates in the forward pass.

blocks.text: 4. Why Freeze Early Layers

blocks.alt: Early layers hold general features and are kept frozen

blocks.text: This connects back to early versus later layer filters, already covered in Filters and Kernels. Genuinely early layers tend to learn genuinely simple, general patterns, already covered there for Convolutional Neural Networks.
These genuinely general patterns often transfer well without needing any genuinely further adjustment, exactly the transferability already covered as general-purpose representations in Pretraining.
5. Later Layers Stay Flexible

blocks.alt: Later layers are task-specific and stay trainable

blocks.text: This connects back to later layer filters, already covered in Filters and Kernels. Genuinely later layers tend to learn increasingly task-specific patterns, already covered there.

These genuinely benefit most from staying genuinely unfrozen, adjustable during Fine-Tuning, letting the model genuinely adapt its own most task-specific representations to the genuinely new, current task.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This early-frozen, later-flexible pattern, already covered in this topic, directly mirrors the early-versus-later layer distinction already covered generally in Filters and Kernels, applied here specifically to the Fine-Tuning process.

blocks.text: 6. A Genuine Computational Saving Benefit

blocks.alt: Frozen layers give faster training and less memory use

blocks.text: A genuinely real, practical benefit connects back to Backpropagation, already covered in its own topic. Frozen layers genuinely still need forward pass computation, but genuinely skip gradient computation entirely.
This is a genuinely real, direct computational saving, since Backpropagation's own genuinely expensive gradient calculations, already covered there, simply never happen for genuinely frozen layers.
7. Reduced Overfitting Risk

This connects back to Overfitting, already covered in its own topic. Fewer genuinely trainable parameters, already covered generally throughout Regularization Techniques, directly reduce overfitting risk.

This is especially genuinely valuable when the Fine-Tuning dataset is genuinely small, already covered as a common, real scenario in Fine-Tuning, directly echoing the Bias-Variance Tradeoff already covered in that earlier module.

blocks.text: 8. Gradual Unfreezing

blocks.alt: All frozen moves to some unfrozen, then all unfrozen

blocks.text: A genuinely practical, real technique connects back to Fine-Tuning's own careful, gradual approach, already covered in that topic. Genuinely start with most layers frozen, then progressively unfreeze more layers as training proceeds.

This genuinely practical, real technique, already covered in this section, offers a genuinely careful middle ground between fully frozen and fully unfrozen Fine-Tuning, already covered throughout the rest of this topic.
9. Recognizing When Frozen Layers Are Genuinely The Right Choice

blocks.alt: A small fine-tuning dataset points toward freezing early layers

blocks.text: This connects back to genuinely small Fine-Tuning datasets, already covered in Fine-Tuning. Frozen Layers, already covered in this topic, directly reduce overfitting risk and computational cost together.

This connects back to catastrophic forgetting, already covered in Fine-Tuning, as a genuinely real risk. Freezing early layers, already covered, directly helps preserve that genuinely valuable prior knowledge.
10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates freezing early layers while keeping later layers trainable, illustrating the concepts already covered throughout this topic.

code.content:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
num_layers = 5
hidden_size = 8

layers = [{"weights": rng.normal(size=(hidden_size, hidden_size)) * 0.02, "frozen": False} for _ in range(num_layers)]

# already covered as why freeze early layers in this topic
freeze_up_to = 3
for i in range(freeze_up_to):
    layers[i]["frozen"] = True

def simulate_gradient_step(layer, learning_rate, rng):
    if layer["frozen"]:  # already covered as what freezing genuinely means in this topic
        return layer["weights"]  # genuinely unchanged, no gradient computation at all
    gradient = rng.normal(size=layer["weights"].shape) * 0.1
    return layer["weights"] - learning_rate * gradient

for i, layer in enumerate(layers):
    original_weights = layer["weights"].copy()
    layer["weights"] = simulate_gradient_step(layer, 1e-4, rng)
    changed = not np.allclose(original_weights, layer["weights"])
    status = "frozen (already covered in this topic)" if layer["frozen"] else "trainable"
    print(f"Layer {i}: {status}, weights changed: {changed}")

blocks.content: Running this example shows the first three layers genuinely staying completely unchanged, while the later, unfrozen layers genuinely update normally, exactly the freezing behavior already covered as this topic's own core mechanism.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Frozen Layers are deliberately kept fixed, unchanged throughout Fine-Tuning.
A frozen layer's weights never get updated, even though gradients still flow through it.
Early layers tend to learn simple, general patterns that often transfer well without adjustment.
Later layers tend to learn task-specific patterns, benefiting most from staying unfrozen.
Frozen layers skip gradient computation entirely, a real computational saving.
Fewer trainable parameters directly reduce overfitting risk, especially with small datasets.
Gradual unfreezing starts with most layers frozen, then progressively unfreezes more over time.
They help preserve valuable pretrained knowledge, reducing catastrophic forgetting risk.
